claims.source: Consistent with this observation, neurons in the ectopia also stained positive for both Ctip2 and Cux1, genes specific to lower- and upper-layer neurons, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claims.claim: In cortical areas without ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, radial migration of early- and late-born neurons appeared largely normal.
claims.source: Interestingly, in cortical areas without ectopia, radial migration of early- and late-born neurons appeared largely normal as shown by birth-dating as well as Cux1 and Ctip2 staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Cell-autonomous defects in neurons are unlikely the cause of the ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: This suggests that cell-autonomous defects in neurons are unlikely the cause of the ectopia.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that neuronal migration appears normal in areas without ectopia.

claims.claim: At E16.5, clear breaches in the pial basement membrane of the developing cortex were apparent in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: At E16.5, clear breaches in the pial basement membrane of the developing cortex were already apparent (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Radial glial fibers in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants extended beyond the breaches in the basement membrane.
claims.source: However, unlike classic models of cobblestone lissencephaly, where radial glial fibers typically retract, radial glial fibers in ric8a mutants instead extended beyond the breaches.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claims.claim: Radial glial cell adhesion defects are unlikely the cause of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: This argues against radial glial cell adhesion defects since they would be predicted to retract.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that radial glial fibers extend beyond breaches rather than retract.

claims.claim: In areas without ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, normal localization of Cajal–Retzius cells was observed.
claims.source: Furthermore, in areas without ectopia, we also observed normal localization of Cajal–Retzius cells, expression of Reelin, and splitting of the preplate, arguing against primary defects in Cajal–Retzius cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claims.claim: Primary defects in Cajal–Retzius cells are unlikely the cause of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, in areas without ectopia, we also observed normal localization of Cajal–Retzius cells, expression of Reelin, and splitting of the preplate, arguing against primary defects in Cajal–Retzius cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of normal Cajal–Retzius cell localization and function.

claims.claim: In Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, large numbers of basement membrane breaches were observed at E14.5, almost all associated with ectopia.
claims.source: In Ric8a mutants, we observed large numbers of basement membrane breaches at E14.5, almost all associated with ectopia (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: At E13.5 in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, significant numbers of basement membrane breaches were observed, but none was associated with ectopia.
claims.source: In contrast, at E13.5, although we also observed significant numbers of breaches, none was associated with ectopia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claims.claim: Basement membrane breaches precede ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: This indicates that basement membrane breaches similarly precede ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of breaches and ectopia formation.

claims.claim: At E12.5 in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, increased numbers of laminin-positive debris were observed across the lateral cortex.
claims.source: However, at E12.5, despite a complete lack of basement membrane breaches, we observed increased numbers of laminin-positive debris across the lateral cortex, both beneath basement membrane segments with intact laminin staining and beneath segments with disrupted laminin staining, the latter presumably sites of future breach (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Excessive basement membrane degradation is likely a primary cause of cortical ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that excessive basement membrane degradation, but not defective maintenance, is likely a primary cause of cortical ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased laminin debris preceding breaches and ectopia.

claims.claim: Deletion of Ric8a by Nestin-Cre did not result in ectopia.
claims.source: To our surprise, deletion of Ric8a by Nestin-Cre did not result in ectopia (Ma et al., 2017; Figure 1g, g').
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and cited previous study.

claims.claim: Combined deletion of Ric8a from neural progenitors, post-mitotic neurons, and astrocytes does not lead to ectopia.
claims.source: Since Nestin-Cre-mediated deletion in neural progenitors is inherited by post-mitotic neurons and astrocytes, this indicates that the combined deletion of Ric8a from all these cell types does not lead to ectopia.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of ectopia in Nestin-Cre mutants.

claims.claim: Ric8a deletion using Foxg1-Cre failed to produce ectopia.
claims.source: We found that Ric8a deletion using Foxg1-Cre still failed to produce ectopia (Figure 1h, h').
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Ric8a deficiency in neural cell lineages is not responsible for basement membrane degradation and ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
claims.source: Thus, these results strongly argue against the interpretation that Ric8a deficiency in neural cell lineages is responsible for basement membrane degradation and ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of ectopia when Ric8a is deleted using various neural-specific Cre lines.

claims.claim: Brain microglia express Emx1 at a significant level.
claims.source: To assess the role of non-neural cell types, we turned our attention to microglia since RNA-seq studies show that brain microglia express Emx1 at a significant level (Zhang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous RNA-seq study.

claims.claim: Emx1-Cre-mediated Ric8a deletion resulted in altered cytokine expression in microglia.
claims.source: We found that Emx1-Cre-mediated Ric8a deletion resulted in altered cytokine expression in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Emx1-Cre is expressed and active in microglia.
claims.source: This indicate that Emx1-Cre is expressed and active in microglia and deletes Ric8a.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of altered cytokine expression in microglia from Emx1-Cre mutants.

claims.claim: When crossed to a reporter, Emx1-Cre resulted in the expression of reporter gene in microglia.
claims.source: In further support of this interpretation, we found that when crossed to a reporter, Emx1-Cre resulted in the expression of reporter gene in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–c'').
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Emx1-Cre resulted in the reduction of Ric8a mRNA levels in microglia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: It also resulted in the reduction of Ric8a mRNA levels in in microglia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia showed elevated cytokine secretion in comparison to control microglia upon LPS stimulation.
claims.source: Like Emx1-Cre mutants, Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia also showed elevated cytokine secretion and transcription in comparison to control microglia upon stimulation by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Figure 2a, b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia showed elevated cytokine transcription in comparison to control microglia upon LPS stimulation.
claims.source: Like Emx1-Cre mutants, Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia also showed elevated cytokine secretion and transcription in comparison to control microglia upon stimulation by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Figure 2a, b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant microglia showed elevated cytokine secretion and transcription upon stimulation by poly I:C.
claims.source: Similar results were also obtained with stimulation by polyinosinic–polycytidylic acid (poly I:C), an intracellular immune activator.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA and qRT-PCR assays.

claims.claim: Ric8a deficiency in microglia results in broad increases in microglial sensitivity to immune stimulation.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that ric8a deficiency in microglia results in broad increases in microglial sensitivity to immune stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of elevated cytokine responses to multiple immune stimuli.

claims.claim: Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants did not show ectopia without LPS treatment.
claims.source: To determine if microglial Ric8a deficiency alone is sufficient to cause cortical ectopia in vivo, we examined Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants but found that it did not affect either basement membrane integrity or cortical layering (Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Over 50% of Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant neonates showed ectopia when administered LPS at E11.5–12.5.
claims.source: We found that over 50% of Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant neonates showed ectopia when administered LPS at E11.5–12.5 (10 of 19 mutant neonates examined) (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: No cortical ectopia were observed in any of the 32 littermate controls that were administered LPS.
claims.source: In contrast, no cortical ectopia were observed in any of the 32 littermate controls that were similarly administered LPS.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from histological analysis.

claims.claim: Only the combination of microglial Ric8a deficiency and immune activation leads to ectopia formation.
claims.source: This indicates that only the combination of microglial Ric8a deficiency and immune activation leads to ectopia formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ectopia only form when both conditions are present.

claims.claim: Ric8a deletion by the dual Cre combination of Cx3cr1-Cre and Nestin-Cre resulted in severe ectopia in all double Cre mutants.
claims.source: However, we found that, like deletion by Emx1-Cre, ric8a deletion by the dual Cre combination of Cx3cr1-Cre and Nestin-Cre also resulted in severe ectopia in all double Cre mutants (six of six examined) (Figure 2f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Elevated immune activation of Ric8a deficient microglia during cortical development is responsible for ectopia formation.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that elevated immune activation of Ric8a deficient microglia during cortical development is responsible for ectopia formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ectopia form when Ric8a-deficient microglia are activated.

claims.claim: The Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant is unique in that ectopia are not observed at the cortical midline but are instead exclusively located to the lateral cortex.
claims.source: There are only a few mutants including the Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant that are exception, in that the ectopia are not observed at the cortical midline but are instead exclusively located to the lateral cortex (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The other mutants with ectopia exclusively in the lateral cortex include the App/Aplp1/2 triple and Apbb1/2 double knockouts.
claims.source: The other mutants in this unique group include the App/Aplp1/2 triple (Herms et al., 2004) and Apbb1/2 double knockouts (Guénette et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Similar mechanisms involving microglia may underlie ectopia formation in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre, App/Aplp1/2, and Apbb1/2 mutants.
claims.source: This suggests that similar mechanisms involving microglia may underlie ectopia formation in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre, App/Aplp1/2, and Apbb1/2 mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of ectopia phenotypes.

claims.claim: Specific App knockdown in cortical neurons during development results in under-migration of targeted neurons.
claims.source: For example, unlike the triple knockout, which causes neuronal over-migration, specific App knockdown in cortical neurons during development results in under- instead of over-migration of targeted neurons (Young-Pearse et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Ric8a-regulated Gα proteins play a conserved role in mediating key branches of APP signaling in cells across species.
claims.source: Furthermore, Ric8a-regulated Gα proteins play a conserved role in mediating key branches of APP signaling in cells across species (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and we confirmed that Gαi proteins are severely depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Gαi proteins are severely depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortices.
claims.source: Furthermore, Ric8a-regulated Gα proteins play a conserved role in mediating key branches of APP signaling in cells across species (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and we confirmed that Gαi proteins are severely depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Microglia cultured from App:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants showed reduced TNFα and IL-6 secretion upon stimulation.
claims.source: To this end, we employed Cx3cr1-Cre to delete a conditional allele of App from microglia and found that microglia cultured from App:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants showed reduced TNFα and IL-6 secretion as well as muted IL-6 transcription upon stimulation (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: App plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia in regulating microglial activity.
claims.source: This indicates that App plays a previously unrecognized, cell-autonomous role in microglia in regulating microglial activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of altered cytokine responses in App mutant microglia.

claims.claim: App mutant peritoneal macrophages showed significantly elevated secretion of all cytokines tested upon LPS stimulation.
claims.source: We found that App mutant macrophages showed significantly elevated secretion of all cytokines tested (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: App mutant peritoneal macrophages showed increased mRNA induction for all cytokines tested upon LPS stimulation.
claims.source: At the transcriptional level, mRNA induction was also increased for all cytokines (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The normal function of App is to suppress the inflammatory activation of microglia.
claims.source: Thus, like that of Ric8a, the normal function of App also appears to be to suppress the inflammatory activation of microglia.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of elevated cytokine responses in App mutant microglia and macrophages.

claims.claim: A significant number of App:Cx3cr1-Cre mutant neonates showed ectopia when administered LPS at E11.5–12.5.
claims.source: We found that, while none of the 81 littermate controls administered LPS showed ectopia, a significant number of mutant neonates showed ectopia (6 of 31 neonates examined, ~19%) and associated breaches in the basement membrane (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–f'').
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: App-deficient microglia, when activated, results in cortical ectopia during development.
claims.source: Thus, app deficient microglia, when activated, also results in cortical ectopia during development.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ectopia form in App mutants when microglia are activated by LPS.

claims.claim: App normally plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia that negatively regulates microglial activation.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that App normally plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia that negatively regulate microglial activation, and its loss of function underlies cortical ectopia formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that App-deficient microglia show elevated activation and cause ectopia when stimulated.

claims.claim: App and Ric8a form a previously unknown anti-inflammatory pathway in microglia.
claims.source: The similarities between App and Ric8a mutant phenotypes suggest that they form a previously unknown anti-inflammatory pathway in microglia.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of phenotypes between App and Ric8a mutants.

claims.claim: Aβ has nanomolar direct binding affinity to APP.
claims.source: Several molecules have been reported to bind to APP and/or activate APP-dependent pathways (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Rice et al., 2012), among which Aβ is noteworthy for its nanomolar direct binding affinity (Fogel et al., 2014; Shaked et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Aβ oligomers and fibrils are pro-inflammatory.
claims.source: Aβ oligomers and fibrils have been shown by numerous studies to be pro-inflammatory, while non-fibrillar Aβ lack such activity (Halle et al., 2008; Huang, 2023; Huang, 2024; Lorton et al., 1996; Muehlhauser et al., 2001; Tan et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Non-fibrillar Aβ lack pro-inflammatory activity.
claims.source: Aβ oligomers and fibrils have been shown by numerous studies to be pro-inflammatory, while non-fibrillar Aβ lack such activity (Halle et al., 2008; Huang, 2023; Huang, 2024; Lorton et al., 1996; Muehlhauser et al., 2001; Tan et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Aβ inhibits T cell activation when employed under conditions that favor the monomer conformation.
claims.source: In contrast, when employed under conditions that favor the monomer conformation, Aβ inhibits T cell activation (Grant et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers potently suppressed the secretion of large numbers of cytokines by microglia.
claims.source: We found that Aβ monomers as prepared potently suppressed the secretion of large numbers of cytokines (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and showed similar effects on microglia no matter if they were activated by LPS or poly I:C (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers showed similar suppressive effects on microglia whether they were activated by LPS or poly I:C.
claims.source: We found that Aβ monomers as prepared potently suppressed the secretion of large numbers of cytokines (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and showed similar effects on microglia no matter if they were activated by LPS or poly I:C (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers strongly inhibited the induction of cytokines at the transcriptional level.
claims.source: We also found that the Aβ monomers similarly strongly inhibited the induction of cytokines at the transcriptional level (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Monomeric Aβ possesses a previously unreported anti-inflammatory activity against microglia.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that monomeric Aβ possesses a previously unreported anti-inflammatory activity against microglia that strongly inhibits microglial inflammatory activation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ monomers suppress cytokine expression by microglia.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers failed to suppress the secretion of all tested cytokines by App mutant microglia.
claims.source: We found that, unlike that of control microglia, Aβ monomers failed to suppress the secretion of all tested cytokines by App mutant microglia (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers still significantly suppressed cytokine secretion by Aplp2 mutant microglia.
claims.source: Interestingly, this blockade appeared to be specific to App since Aβ monomers still significantly suppressed cytokine secretion by Aplp2 mutant microglia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA assays.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers failed to suppress cytokine induction in App mutant microglia at the transcriptional level.
claims.source: At the transcriptional level, Aβ monomers also failed to suppress cytokine induction in App mutant microglia (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: APP is functionally required in microglia for Aβ monomer inhibition of cytokine expression at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that APP is functionally required in microglia for Aβ monomer inhibition of cytokine expression at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ monomers fail to suppress cytokine expression in App mutant microglia.

claims.claim: Cytokine secretion by control macrophages was strongly suppressed by Aβ monomers.
claims.source: We found that, like that of control microglia, cytokine secretion by control macrophages was also strongly suppressed by Aβ monomers (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: App mutant macrophages failed to respond to Aβ monomers.
claims.source: However, even though App mutant macrophages showed elevated response to immune stimulation in comparison to control macrophages, they still failed to respond to Aβ monomers and displayed levels of cytokine secretion that were indistinguishable from those of DMSO-treated cells (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: APP function is required in microglia for mediating the anti-inflammatory effects of Aβ monomers.
claims.source: Thus, these results further indicate that APP function is required in microglia for mediating the anti-inflammatory effects of Aβ monomers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that App mutant macrophages fail to respond to Aβ monomers.

claims.claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins are coupled to APP and mediate APP intracellular signaling in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that heterotrimeric G proteins are coupled to APP and mediate APP intracellular signaling in vitro and vivo (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and that Ric8a is a molecular chaperone essential for the post-translational stability of heterotrimeric G proteins (Gabay et al., 2011; Tall et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Ric8a is a molecular chaperone essential for the post-translational stability of heterotrimeric G proteins.
claims.source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that heterotrimeric G proteins are coupled to APP and mediate APP intracellular signaling in vitro and vivo (Fogel et al., 2014; Milosch et al., 2014; Nishimoto et al., 1993; Ramaker et al., 2013) and that Ric8a is a molecular chaperone essential for the post-translational stability of heterotrimeric G proteins (Gabay et al., 2011; Tall et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers failed to suppress the secretion of TNFα and IL-6 by Ric8a mutant microglia.
claims.source: We found that, indeed, like that of App mutant microglia, Aβ monomers also failed to suppress the secretion of TNFα and IL-6 by Ric8a mutant microglia (Figure 4g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Heterotrimeric G protein function is likely required in the same pathway as APP in microglia for the suppression of TNFα and IL-6 secretion.
claims.source: This indicates that heterotrimeric G proteins function is likely required in the same pathway of APP in microglia for the suppression of TNFα and IL-6 secretion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ monomers fail to suppress TNFα and IL-6 secretion in Ric8a mutant microglia.

claims.claim: Aβ monomers still suppressed IL-1β secretion by Ric8a mutant microglia.
claims.source: However, unlike APP, we found that Ric8a appears to be dispensable for Aβ monomer regulation of other cytokines. For example, unlike that of TNFα and IL-6, Aβ monomers still suppressed IL-1β secretion by Ric8a mutant microglia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Ric8a is dispensable for Aβ monomer regulation of cytokine transcription.
claims.source: It also appears to be dispensable for the regulation of cytokine transcription since Aβ monomers similarly suppressed IL-6 transcriptional induction in both control and Ric8a mutant microglia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR assays.

claims.claim: Heterotrimeric G protein function may only mediate some of the anti-inflammatory signaling of monomeric Aβ.
claims.source: These results suggest that heterotrimeric G proteins function may only mediate some of the anti-inflammatory signaling of monomeric Aβ.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ric8a is dispensable for some but not all Aβ monomer effects.

claims.claim: APP and Ric8a-regulated heterotrimeric G proteins form part of a novel anti-inflammatory pathway activated by monomeric Aβ in microglia.
claims.source: Thus, APP and Ric8a-regulated heterotrimeric G proteins form part of a novel anti-inflammatory pathway activated by monomeric Aβ in microglia.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both APP and Ric8a are required for some Aβ monomer effects.

claims.claim: Dorsomorphin and S3I-201 suppressed astrogliosis associated with neuroinflammation in the cortex of Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: Consistent with their anti-inflammatory activity, we found that dorsomorphin and S3I-201 both suppressed astrogliosis associated with neuroinflammation in the cortex of Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Dorsomorphin and S3I-201 suppressed the formation of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, they also suppressed the formation of ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, reducing both the number and the size of the ectopia observed (Figure 5a–f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The combined administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 nearly eliminated all ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: Most strikingly, the combined administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 nearly eliminated all ectopia in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 5d, e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Excessive inflammatory activation of microglia is responsible for ectopia formation in Ric8a mutants.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that excessive inflammatory activation of microglia is responsible for ectopia formation in ric8a mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that anti-inflammatory drugs suppress ectopia formation.

claims.claim: At E13.5, MMP9 mRNA is strongly expressed in a sparse cell population resembling microglia populating the cortex.
claims.source: We found that at E13.5, MMP9 mRNA is strongly expressed in a sparse cell population resembling microglia populating the cortex at this stage (Squarzoni et al., 2014; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and a citation.

claims.claim: The activity of MMP9 in the mutant cortex was significantly increased.
claims.source: We found that the activity of MMP9 in the mutant cortex was significantly increased (Figure 5i, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The activity of MMP2 remained unaffected in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: In contrast, that activity of MMP2 remained unaffected.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gel zymography.

claims.claim: The immunoreactivity for MMP9 was increased in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
claims.source: Similarly, at the protein level, we found that the immunoreactivity for MMP9 was increased in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants (Figure 5g, h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: BB94 administration significantly suppressed both the number and the size of the ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
claims.source: We found that BB94 administration significantly suppress both the number and the size of the ectopia in ric8a mutants (Figure 5j–m).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: MMP-9/MMP-13 inhibitor I significantly suppressed both the number and the size of the ectopia in Ric8a mutants.
claims.source: To narrow down the identity of MMPs responsible, we further employed an inhibitor specific for MMP9 and 13 (MMP-9/MMP-13 inhibitor I, CAS 204140-01-2) and found that it similarly suppressed both the number and the size of the ectopia (Figure 5l, m).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Co-administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 reduced MMP9 activity in the mutant cortex to the control level.
claims.source: Furthermore, consistent with its near complete suppression of cortical ectopia (Figure 5a–f), we found that the co-administration of dorsomorphin and S3I-201 also reduced MMP9 activity in the mutant cortex to the control level (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The Aβ monomer-regulated anti-inflammatory pathway normally promotes cortical development through suppressing microglial activation and MMP induction.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate this Aβ monomer-regulated anti-inflammatory pathway normally promotes cortical development through suppressing microglial activation and MMP induction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that inhibiting microglial activation or MMP activity suppresses ectopia formation.

claims.claim: Microglial activity has been found to regulate the size of the cortical neural precursor pool.
claims.source: Indeed, microglial activity has been found to regulate the size of the cortical neural precursor pool (Cunningham et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Microglia-secreted cytokines have been found to promote both neurogenesis and oligodendrogenesis.
claims.source: Microglia-secreted cytokines have also been found to promote both neurogenesis and oligodendrogenesis (Shigemoto-Mogami et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Reductions in the expression of microglial immune and chemotaxis genes lead to the failure of microglia to populate the brain.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that reductions in the expression of microglial immune and chemotaxis genes instead lead to the failure of microglia to populate the brain (Iyer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins directly interact with the APP cytoplasmic domain.

results.result: Deletion of Ric8a using Emx1-Cre results in cortical ectopia formation exclusively in the lateral cortex, preceded by basement membrane breaches and increased laminin debris. The ectopia contain both early- and late-born neurons, but neuronal migration appears normal in areas without ectopia, suggesting that excessive basement membrane degradation rather than cell-autonomous neuronal defects is the primary cause.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C47 provide converging evidence from multiple developmental timepoints (E12.5-E16.5) showing temporal progression from laminin debris (C46) to breaches (C43-C45) to ectopia (C33). The observation that neuronal migration is normal in unaffected areas (C36) and that radial glial fibers extend rather than retract (C39-C40) effectively rules out cell-autonomous neuronal defects, supporting the conclusion of excessive degradation (C47).

results.result: Deletion of Ric8a using neural-specific Cre lines (Nestin-Cre and Foxg1-Cre) does not result in ectopia, indicating that Ric8a deficiency in neural cell lineages is not responsible for the phenotype observed with Emx1-Cre.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 provide clear negative results with multiple neural-specific Cre lines that should delete Ric8a from neural progenitors and their progeny. The lack of ectopia in these mutants (C48, C50) combined with the logical inference (C49, C51) strongly argues against neural cell-autonomous mechanisms.

results.result: Emx1-Cre is expressed and active in microglia, and Ric8a deletion in microglia using either Emx1-Cre or the microglia-specific Cx3cr1-Cre results in elevated cytokine secretion and transcription upon immune stimulation with LPS or poly I:C.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C60 provide multiple lines of evidence for microglial Emx1-Cre activity (reporter expression C55, reduced Ric8a mRNA C56, altered cytokine expression C53) and demonstrate elevated immune responses in both Emx1-Cre and Cx3cr1-Cre mutants (C57-C59) with multiple stimuli, supporting broad microglial hyperactivation (C60).

results.result: Microglial Ric8a deficiency alone is insufficient to cause ectopia, but the combination of Ric8a deficiency and immune activation (via LPS administration or dual deletion with Nestin-Cre) results in ectopia formation, indicating that elevated immune activation of Ric8a-deficient microglia is responsible for the phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C66 demonstrate a clear requirement for both Ric8a deficiency and immune activation. The negative result without LPS (C61), positive result with LPS in mutants but not controls (C62-C63), and positive result with dual Cre deletion (C65) provide strong evidence for the two-hit model (C64, C66).

results.result: APP plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia in suppressing inflammatory activation. App deletion in microglia using Cx3cr1-Cre results in altered cytokine responses in cultured microglia and elevated cytokine secretion in fresh peritoneal macrophages. When combined with LPS administration during development, App-deficient microglia cause cortical ectopia.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C80 provide consistent evidence across multiple experimental systems (cultured microglia C73, fresh macrophages C75-C76, in vivo development C78) showing that App loss leads to microglial hyperactivation and ectopia formation when activated. The use of fresh macrophages (C75-C76) addresses potential culture artifacts noted for microglia (C73).

results.result: The Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant shares a unique phenotype with App/Aplp1/2 triple and Apbb1/2 double knockouts—ectopia exclusively in the lateral cortex. Ric8a-regulated Gαi proteins are severely depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants and play conserved roles in APP signaling, suggesting that App and Ric8a form a previously unknown anti-inflammatory pathway in microglia.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 and C81 establish phenotypic similarity (C67-C68), provide mechanistic links through Gα protein depletion (C72) and known APP-Gα interactions (C71), and exclude neuronal cell-autonomous mechanisms (C70). The convergence of genetic, biochemical, and phenotypic evidence supports the pathway model (C81).

results.result: Monomeric Aβ potently suppresses cytokine secretion and transcription by microglia activated with either LPS or poly I:C, demonstrating a previously unreported anti-inflammatory activity of Aβ monomers against microglia.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 provide clear dose-response data showing suppression of multiple cytokines at both protein (C86) and mRNA (C88) levels with two different immune stimuli (C87). The consistency across multiple cytokines and stimuli strongly supports the novel anti-inflammatory activity (C89).

results.result: APP is functionally required in microglia for Aβ monomer-mediated suppression of cytokine expression. Aβ monomers fail to suppress cytokine secretion and transcription in App mutant microglia and macrophages, while retaining activity in Aplp2 mutants, indicating APP-specific requirement.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C96 demonstrate loss of Aβ monomer activity in App mutants across multiple cell types (cultured microglia C90-C92, fresh macrophages C94-C95) and multiple cytokines, while showing specificity through retained activity in Aplp2 mutants (C91). The use of fresh macrophages (C94-C95) addresses potential culture artifacts.

results.result: Heterotrimeric G proteins function in the same pathway as APP in microglia for Aβ monomer-mediated suppression of some but not all cytokines. Aβ monomers fail to suppress TNFα and IL-6 secretion in Ric8a mutant microglia but still suppress IL-1β secretion and cytokine transcription, suggesting that G proteins mediate only some branches of Aβ monomer anti-inflammatory signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 show selective loss of Aβ monomer activity for specific cytokines (TNFα, IL-6) but not others (IL-1β) in Ric8a mutants (C99, C101), and retention of transcriptional effects (C102). This cytokine-specific pattern (C103) supports a model where G proteins mediate some but not all Aβ signaling branches (C104).

results.result: Anti-inflammatory drugs (dorsomorphin and S3I-201) suppress astrogliosis and ectopia formation in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants, with combined treatment nearly eliminating all ectopia, indicating that excessive inflammatory activation of microglia is responsible for ectopia formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 provide pharmacological validation of the inflammatory mechanism through dose-dependent suppression of both astrogliosis (C105) and ectopia (C106), with near-complete rescue by combined treatment (C107). This pharmacological evidence strongly supports the causal role of microglial inflammation (C108).

results.result: MMP9 is expressed in microglia-like cells in the developing cortex and its activity is significantly increased in Ric8a mutants. Pharmacological inhibition of MMPs (BB94 or MMP9/13-specific inhibitor) significantly suppresses ectopia formation, and anti-inflammatory drug treatment reduces MMP9 activity to control levels, indicating that the Aβ monomer-regulated pathway promotes cortical development by suppressing microglial activation and MMP induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116 establish MMP9 as a key downstream effector through expression pattern (C109), increased activity in mutants (C110-C112), pharmacological rescue with MMP inhibitors (C113-C114), and normalization by anti-inflammatory treatment (C115). The convergence of expression, activity, and rescue data strongly supports the mechanistic model (C116).

results.result: Aβ forms aggregates in the Alzheimer's disease brain and also regulates neuronal physiology in the healthy brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 represent well-established background knowledge (C1) and cite recent literature (C2) to set up the context for the study. These are appropriately supported by established knowledge and citations.

results.result: Aβ oligomers are highly toxic with wide-ranging effects including inhibition of neurotransmitter release, depletion of synaptic vesicle pools, disruption of postsynaptic organization and function, and impairment of synaptic plasticity, which likely underpin the pathogenic role of Aβ in Alzheimer's disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 summarize well-established literature on Aβ oligomer toxicity with extensive citations (C13-C17). The inference about pathogenic role (C18) is reasonable given the cited evidence, though it remains an inference rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: Aβ is produced in the healthy brain by neurons in an activity-dependent manner and regulates normal neuronal physiology. Aβ monomers and low-molecular-weight oligomers positively regulate synaptic function and plasticity, and their administration improves learning and memory in animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 provide literature-based context for physiological Aβ functions with multiple citations. These establish the rationale for investigating Aβ monomer functions beyond toxicity.

results.result: Microglia and astrocytes play critical roles in brain development, function, and plasticity by coordinately regulating spatiotemporally specific expression of immune cytokines. Examples include IL-33 regulation in thalamus and hippocampus, TNFα regulation in striatum and neocortex, and roles in clinical applications and disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C32 provide comprehensive literature-based background on glial cytokine regulation with appropriate citations. These establish the biological context and significance of the study's focus on microglial regulation.

results.result: Aβ has nanomolar binding affinity to APP. Aβ oligomers and fibrils are pro-inflammatory while non-fibrillar Aβ lacks such activity. Under conditions favoring monomers, Aβ inhibits T cell activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 provide literature-based rationale for investigating Aβ monomers as potential APP ligands with anti-inflammatory activity. The citations support the binding affinity (C82), differential activities of oligomers vs monomers (C83-C84), and precedent for monomer anti-inflammatory activity (C85).

results.result: Heterotrimeric G proteins are coupled to APP and mediate APP intracellular signaling in vitro and in vivo. Ric8a is a molecular chaperone essential for the post-translational stability of heterotrimeric G proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 provide well-cited background on APP-G protein interactions and Ric8a function, establishing the mechanistic rationale for investigating the APP-Ric8a pathway.

results.result: Microglial activity regulates the cortical neural precursor pool size, microglia-secreted cytokines promote neurogenesis and oligodendrogenesis, and reductions in microglial immune gene expression lead to failure of microglia to populate the brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 provide cited literature context for the importance of precise microglial activity regulation during development, supporting the significance of the findings.

results.result: Heterotrimeric G proteins directly interact with the APP cytoplasmic domain and mediate APP signaling across species. Pancortin, an olfactomedin family protein that inhibits innate immunity, is expressed in the early cortex and may serve as an APP ligand.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C122 provide literature-based discussion of alternative APP ligands and signaling mechanisms, appropriately acknowledging that other ligands besides Aβ may activate the pathway in vivo.

results.result: Nestin-Cre expression is influenced by transgene insertion site and genetic background, and has been reported to be active in microglia in some contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 provide cited discussion of potential technical factors that could explain discrepancies between studies regarding Nestin-Cre activity in microglia.

results.result: Aβ is produced by neurons in an activity-dependent manner and forms oligomers when produced in large quantities. Aβ oligomers are pro-inflammatory and increase glial cytokine expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 provide cited background on activity-dependent Aβ production and oligomer formation, establishing the basis for the discussion of how neural activity levels may differentially regulate glial cytokine expression.

results.result: Aβ and related pathways mediate homeostatic and competitive plasticity in the visual and other brain systems. MMP9 is a pivotal mediator of TNFα-dependent homeostatic synaptic upscaling in visual cortex, is induced by neural activity, promotes dendritic growth, and can reactivate adult visual cortex plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C136 provide extensive cited literature connecting Aβ pathways to synaptic plasticity and establishing MMP9 as a key mediator of activity-dependent plasticity, supporting the broader significance of the findings.

results.result: Aβ monomers are directly protective to neurons and positively regulate synapse development and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C138 provide cited literature supporting protective roles of Aβ monomers, aligning with and contextualizing the study's findings of anti-inflammatory monomer activity.

results.result: Formation of Aβ oligomers and aggregates would be predicted to deplete Aβ monomers by chemical law. In Alzheimer's disease, there may be depletion of Aβ monomers that contributes to neuroinflammation and neuronal damage. High soluble brain Aβ42 preserves cognition in Alzheimer's patients despite increasing amyloidosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 present a speculative hypothesis about Aβ monomer depletion in Alzheimer's disease. While the chemical principle (C139) and clinical observations (C141) are cited, the causal connection to disease pathogenesis (C140) remains speculative and would require additional experimental validation.

results.result: In neurodegenerative diseases, MMP9 regulates selective neuronal degeneration, is upregulated in plasma of mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's patients, and its reduction protects neurons in motor neuron disease models.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 provide cited literature connecting MMP9 to neurodegenerative disease, supporting the potential clinical relevance of the findings.

results.result: A novel signaling pathway activated by monomeric Aβ plays essential roles in regulating microglial activity and cortical assembly during mouse development. The pathway depends on APP and Ric8a function in microglia and inhibits microglial immune activation at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels. Genetic disruption results in microglial dysregulation, excessive matrix proteinase activation, basement membrane degradation, neuronal ectopia, and laminar disruption.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C11 represent the main findings of the study, summarizing the discovery of the pathway (C3-C5), its disruption phenotypes (C6-C10), and functional interpretation (C11). These are well-supported by the detailed experimental evidence presented in the grouped claims above.

results.result: Aβ monomer depletion may play a role in the development of Alzheimer's disease.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 is explicitly speculative, highlighting a potential overlooked role of Aβ monomer depletion in Alzheimer's disease. While the study establishes that Aβ monomers have anti-inflammatory activity, the causal connection to Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: Following sensory deprivation, Aβ levels may be lowered, leading to relief of monomeric Aβ inhibition of cytokines like TNFα and triggering homeostatic upscaling of cortical synapses. Conversely, high neural activity may produce Aβ oligomers that induce cytokines promoting synaptic pruning.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 present speculative models for how Aβ monomers and oligomers might mediate activity-dependent synaptic plasticity. While these are logical extensions of the findings and cite supporting literature (C129), they remain hypothetical mechanisms requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Ric8a deletion using Emx1-Cre results in ectopia formation exclusively in the lateral cortex, with basement membrane breaches preceding ectopia. The authors claim that cell-autonomous neuronal defects and radial glial adhesion defects are unlikely causes, based on observations that neuronal migration appears normal in areas without ectopia and that radial glial fibers extend beyond breaches rather than retract.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 challenges the interpretation that neuronal defects are not responsible, noting that 'the graph of BrdU cell distribution in the mutant mice (Fig. S1 F) shows that there are more BrdU cells in bins 5-7 and less in bin 9, indicating an impaired migration of upper cortical neurons' and that 'these experiments cannot rule out the possibility of cell-autonomous effect of Ric8a deletion in glutamatergic neurons or radial glial cells.' The reviewers question whether the evidence sufficiently excludes cell-autonomous effects.

results.result: Deletion of Ric8a using Nestin-Cre or Foxg1-Cre did not result in ectopia, leading authors to conclude that Ric8a deficiency in neural cell lineages is not responsible for basement membrane degradation and ectopia.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly challenges this conclusion, stating 'NestinCre and Emx1Cre mouse models are targeting the same type of cells in the developing cortex (cortical progenitors, glutamatergic neurons and astrocytes), but with one day difference in expression (Emx1 E9.5 and Nestin E10.5)' and 'There is no evidence to assume that ric8a deficiency in neural cell lineages is not responsible for basement membrane degradation and ectopia formation in ric8a mutants.' The reviewers find the evidence insufficient to support this claim.

results.result: The authors claim that Emx1-Cre is expressed and active in microglia, based on altered cytokine expression, reporter gene expression, and reduced Ric8a mRNA levels in microglia from Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'There is no evidence that microglia express Emx1. The paper they referred (Zhang et al., 2014) was performed in adult mice so it is not comparable. Moreover, many other papers are saying that Emx1 is not expressed in microglia.' The reviewer also notes 'change in cytokine expression is not a strong evidence to state that Emx1 is expressed in microglia' and questions why there is only 'partial reduction of Ric8a mRNA levels in Emx1-Ric8a cKO and not a completed deletion.' The evidence is considered weak and inconsistent.

results.result: Ric8a-deficient microglia show elevated cytokine responses to immune stimulation in vitro. When combined with LPS administration in vivo, Ric8a:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants develop ectopia, while neither condition alone produces ectopia. The authors conclude that elevated immune activation of Ric8a-deficient microglia during cortical development is responsible for ectopia formation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Additional experiments should be performed to demonstrate that ectopia formation in Emx1-ric8a cKO mutant mice is due to an increase in immune stimulation and not a cell-autonomous effect. Using double cx3cr1-cre and nestin-cre ric8a mutant mice is not an argument to say that elevated immune activation of ric8a deficient microglia during cortical development is responsible for ectopia formation.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The authors did not provide a control experiment to show that the insult induced by LPS injection does not induce the phenotype in the ric8a-foxg1-cre mice.' The evidence is considered incomplete.

results.result: App-deficient microglia and macrophages show altered cytokine responses to immune stimulation in vitro. When App:Cx3cr1-Cre mutants are administered LPS, a significant number develop ectopia. The authors conclude that App plays a cell-autonomous role in microglia that negatively regulates microglial activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'The authors demonstrated that Abeta monomers are anti-inflammatory and inhibit microglial activation. This is a novel result that demonstrates the physiological role of APP in cortical development.' The in vitro data showing altered cytokine responses in App mutant microglia and the in vivo ectopia formation following LPS treatment are accepted as supporting evidence for APP's role in microglia.

results.result: The authors claim that App and Ric8a form a previously unknown anti-inflammatory pathway in microglia, based on similarities between App and Ric8a mutant phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'The similarities between Ric8a cKO and APP cKO mice are not enough evidence to claim that APP and Ric8a are involved in the same anti-inflammatory pathway in microglia.' The evidence is considered insufficient to support this claim.

results.result: In vitro experiments show that Aβ monomers potently suppress cytokine secretion and transcription by microglia and macrophages. This suppression requires APP but shows differential dependence on Ric8a for different cytokines. The authors conclude that APP and Ric8a-regulated heterotrimeric G proteins form part of a novel anti-inflammatory pathway activated by monomeric Aβ in microglia.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 emphasizes the critical limitation: 'They do not have any proof that Abeta is the activating signal in vivo. Whatever they showed in vitro should be confirmed in vivo to make such a strong claim. The authors even recognized it in their responses to reviewers: "we currently do not have evidence that in the developing cortex Abeta monomers play a role in inhibiting microglia".' Reviewer 1 acknowledges the in vitro findings as novel but the overall evaluation is uncertain due to lack of in vivo validation.

results.result: Administration of anti-inflammatory drugs (dorsomorphin and S3I-201) suppressed astrogliosis and ectopia formation in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutants. The authors conclude that excessive inflammatory activation of microglia is responsible for ectopia formation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 challenges this interpretation: 'This is incorrect. Inhibition of Akt or stat3 does much more than just being pro-inflammatory. This could affect directly migration. The data only show that Akt and/or Stat3 might be involved.' The conclusion is considered an overstatement given the pleiotropic effects of these inhibitors.

results.result: MMP9 activity is significantly increased in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortex, while MMP2 remains unaffected. MMP inhibitors (BB94 and MMP-9/MMP-13 inhibitor I) significantly suppressed ectopia formation. The authors conclude that the Aβ monomer-regulated anti-inflammatory pathway promotes cortical development through suppressing microglial activation and MMP induction.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises methodological concerns: 'Gel zymography is not the same as Western blot. For the quantification of the relative amount of protein, authors should use western blot and not immunofluorescence intensity as shown in Fig. 5g, h.' Reviewer 2 notes the overstatement: 'There is no proof that Abeta is involved in vivo.' The MMP data are accepted but the connection to Aβ monomers in vivo is not established.

results.result: The authors describe a novel signaling pathway activated by monomeric Aβ in vitro that plays essential roles in regulating microglial activity and neocortex assembly during mouse development in vivo. Genetic disruption leads to microglial dysregulation, excessive matrix proteinase activation, basement membrane degradation, neuronal ectopia, and laminar disruption.
results.evaluation: The editor and reviewers acknowledge 'valuable findings that have theoretical and practical implications in the field of neuronal migration, neuronal ectopia and type II lissencephaly' but state 'the evidence is incomplete.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'They do not have any proof that Abeta is the activating signal in vivo' and that the title and abstract are 'misleading, not supported by the data.' The in vivo developmental phenotypes are accepted, but the connection to Aβ monomers as the activating signal is not established.

results.result: The Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant shows ectopia exclusively in the lateral cortex, similar to App/Aplp1/2 triple and Apbb1/2 double knockouts. The authors suggest similar mechanisms involving microglia may underlie ectopia formation in these mutants, supported by evidence that Ric8a-regulated Gαi proteins play conserved roles in APP signaling and are depleted in Ric8a:Emx1-Cre mutant cortices.
results.evaluation: These claims are primarily descriptive and comparative, drawing on established literature about APP signaling and Gαi proteins. The reviewers do not challenge these specific observations or the depletion of Gαi proteins in the mutants. The speculation about similar mechanisms is appropriately framed as a suggestion rather than a definitive conclusion.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate claims C33-C47 about temporal progression of basement membrane defects and exclusion of cell-autonomous neuronal defects. OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED, concluding that converging evidence effectively rules out neuronal defects. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, noting that BrdU distribution data show impaired migration of upper cortical neurons and that experiments cannot definitively rule out cell-autonomous effects in glutamatergic neurons or radial glial cells.

Both evaluate claims C48-C51 about neural-specific Cre lines and exclusion of neural cell-autonomous mechanisms. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED with clear negative results. Peer reviewers rate this UNSUPPORTED, arguing that NestinCre and Emx1Cre target the same cell types with only one day difference in expression timing, and that there is insufficient evidence to exclude neural cell lineage responsibility for the phenotype.

Both evaluate claims C52-C56 about Emx1-Cre activity in microglia. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED based on reporter expression, reduced Ric8a mRNA, and altered cytokine expression. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, challenging the evidence that microglia express Emx1, noting the cited paper used adult mice and that many papers state Emx1 is not expressed in microglia, and questioning why Ric8a deletion is only partial.

Both evaluate the two-hit model requiring Ric8a deficiency and immune activation (C61-C66, with peer review also including C57-C60). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED with clear requirement for both conditions. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, stating that additional experiments are needed to demonstrate ectopia is due to immune stimulation rather than cell-autonomous effects, and noting lack of control experiments showing LPS alone does not induce phenotype in ric8a-foxg1-cre mice.
